overall: The AG found the Wayland School Committee violated the OML by citing wrong or inapplicable executive session purposes for most 2014 METCO sessions, so it could not rely on the OML to withhold those minutes; the February 6 session was proper.

allegations.summary: Complainant alleged the committee improperly withheld minutes of its January 21 and 27, 2014 executive sessions about the METCO matter.
allegations.key_passage: Because the Committee did not follow proper procedure in convening the executive sessions held on January 6, 9, 13, 21, and 27, 2014, and February 3, 2014, the Committee may not rely on the Open Meeting Law as the basis for continuing to withhold the minutes of those executive sessions.

allegations.summary: Complainant alleged the committee held executive sessions for an improper purpose; the committee cited wrong statutory purposes for several January-March 2014 sessions.
allegations.key_passage: This failure violated the Open Meeting Law, as it did not give the public proper notice of what would be discussed behind closed doors.

allegations.summary: Complainant alleged the committee improperly redacted portions of executive session minutes from the METCO-related 2014 meetings released in response to a public records request.
allegations.key_passage: Because the Committee did not follow proper procedure in convening the executive sessions held on January 6, 9, 13, 21, and 27, 2014, and February 3, 2014, the Committee may not rely on the Open Meeting Law as the basis for continuing to withhold the minutes of those executive sessions.

allegations.summary: Challenge to the February 6, 2014 executive session, held under the criminal-investigation purpose, and to withholding its minutes.

remedy: Immediate and future compliance with the Open Meeting Law.
Review the Attorney General's Open Meeting Law training video on executive sessions (Video #4).

remedy_passage: We order the Committee's immediate and future compliance with the Open Meeting Law, and we caution that future similar violations may be considered evidence of intent to violate the law.
